speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prince Albert):
subsubtopic: INLAND SHIPPING-LABOUR DISPUTE INVOLVING MARINE ENGINEERS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing public necessity, namely, that unless the strike of the 800 maritime engineers and deck officers which has stopped shipping on the Great Lakes is ended without delay, it has been estimated by the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool that 150 million bushels of wheat that were to be shipped on the Great Lakes between now and the end of the shipping season will not be shipped, thereby resulting in the catastrophic loss of $400 million to western farmers and a most serious blow to the economy of the western provinces.
I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Wise):
That as the seriousness of the situation will not brook further delay, the government should forthwith introduce legislation to end this strike.

ARTS, LETTERS AND SCIENCES SALARIES OF ACTORS AND ACTRESSES-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43

speechtext:

Given the fact that the bilingualism bonus has always been an incentive for employees who have to work in both official languages either in the public service or in the House of Commons, that abolition of this bonus is unfair to those who invested their time in learning the other language and considering also that Francophones are more penalized by this since they represent the majority of those receiving bonuses, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Allard):
That the House urge the government to change its decision and to maintain the bilingualism bonus program until 1983 as it was previously set up.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to ask for unanimous consent of the House to move a motion on a matter of urgency and national interest.
In view of the announced intention of the government to close the Petawawa forestry station as of next March 31, in view of the nationwide importance of this station for forestry research and development in the country, and also in view of the fact that this decision contradicts the decision taken by the Ministry of State for Science and Technology to give national priority to research and development, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier):

subsubtopic: MOVEMENT OF GRAIN ON GREAT LAKES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question follows the excellent motion presented under Standing Order 43 by the right hon. member for Prince Albert which was rejected by the Minister of Transport and his colleagues on the other side.

subsubtopic: MOVEMENT OF GRAIN ON GREAT LAKES

The answer to that question is yes, of course there was. For a number of days I have been in constant touch with the parties and with people associated with this problem, keeping myself informed as to where the matter stood. I must say it was a great surprise to me that members of the opposition did not appear to know that this threat was even
October 18, 1978

impending, though it had been building up for three months. We were aware of the situation. It was one of disagreement between employer and employee organizations as to the level at which a settlement should take place. There was a conciliator's report which was not acceptable to the parties as a solution to the dispute.
Members of the opposition, in their irresponsibility, need not say whether they agree or disagree with the conciliator's report or with the position taken by the employers or by the employees. They simply called for action. They do not even suggest what action we should take. Are they saying we should not follow the collective bargaining route?

subsubtopic: MOVEMENT OF GRAIN ON GREAT LAKES

subsubtopic: MOVEMENT OF GRAIN ON GREAT LAKES
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker, we carried out an assessment along those lines as we began to learn about the problem. As I have indicated in the House, the damage is very serious. At this very moment discussions are going on. As the hon. member has mentioned, I am rarely excited, but I am always an optimist and I am optimistic that we shall see a settlement later this day.

speechtext:

subsubtopic: IMPACT OF CANADA WORKS PROGRAM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Employment and Immigration. A recent government study indicates that the impact of the government's Canada Works program on the total unemployment scene is not very significant. I should like to ask the minister whether, first of all, he is aware of the study by his department and, further, whether he concurs with the findings of the evaluation committee.

speakeroldname: Hon. Bud Cullen (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subsubtopic: IMPACT OF CANADA WORKS PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at a time of high unemployment it is incumbent upon the government, of whatever political stripe, to come up with direct job-creation programs such as Canada Works and Young Canada Works. But not being satisfied with that, it seems to me that it would be appropriate to make more effective use of the funding we used in these temporary make-work programs. So on that basis we established an economic growth component factor so that we can create permanent jobs, and two provinces to date are benefiting from the forestry program in job creation.
We have the emergency response feature which has helped in particular one-industry towns where some people have suddenly found themselves unemployed, and we have been able to put that program in place. We are gradually moving from a temporary job operation to more permanent job creation. So the weaknesses in those temporary programs have been recognized. That is why we are trying to strengthen them with more long-term job creation programs in co-operation with the provinces.

subsubtopic: IMPACT OF CANADA WORKS PROGRAM
speechtext: In view of that re-evaluation of Canada Works which is taking place, and in view of the fact that the government has spent half a billion dollars from early 1977 on Canada Works projects, I should like to ask the minister whether some of that money in this fiscal year will be redirected to the job creation he has mentioned, namely, long-term jobs in the private sector apart from Canada Works?

subsubtopic: IMPACT OF CANADA WORKS PROGRAM
speechtext:
We announced, I think early in September, something like 14 or 15 different programs which are in place to help with direct job creation, and we are working in close concert with private enterprise. The funding that we saved from the Canada Works program means, of course, that more money is available to be redirected to areas where I think we could create more permanent jobs which would have a more long-term, positive impact on the employment picture.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. Earlier in the afternoon the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner), answering a question from the opposition, conveyed some information which I think is inaccurate and I should like to give him the opportunity either to correct me or correct the impression he left.
In reply to a question he said that, if you look at Canadian exports, the recent figures showed that we were sending out of the country some 10 per cent in agriculture, 20 per cent in oil, gas and minerals, and some 70 per cent in end products and prefabricated goods.

If you compare those two combined as a percentage of our total exports it comes out to only about one-third of them, which is the figure which came roughly to my mind of manufactured or end products only making up about one-third of our exports. Beyond that, of course, we had a deficit in manufacturing trade of some $11 billion in manufactured products in 1977.
I should like the minister to take this opportunity to expand on what he included in those earlier figures. Certainly it was my impression and, I think, the impression of most people who follow trade patterns in Canada, that just the opposite situation exists to the impression he wants to leave-that we continue to rely on the export of unfinished goods instead of finished goods.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, l do not know if it is appropriate to raise a point of order at this time with respect to House business. I will take Your Honour's advice, but there is a matter which came up just before the vote, and I think it is something which ought to be explored here in the House.
Just before the bells began to ring for the vote the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) rose in his place and announced that we would be breaking off the throne speech debate as of tomorrow and that we would be proceeding with government business. It is his right to do that if that is his wish, but I regret to say that is is not in keeping nor in accordance with the undertaking which he gave in the House on October 12 when we discussed the question of House business. We were talking on that day about a possible House leaders' meeting, and I asked whether he was planning a meeting of House leaders to discuss, among other things, the length of the throne speech debate and the order of the business of the House so that the House could, in the words of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), get down to the business of legislating.
The Deputy Prime Minister said in reply that there would be a House leaders' meeting on the following Wednesday. There has been no such House leaders' meeting.
I raise this matter for two reasons. The Deputy Prime Minister has announced the intention of breaking off the throne speech debate which, as I said, he can do, but we are left in limbo as to the question of whether the throne speech debate is ever to be terminated. I think the House is entitled to some clarification with respect to that because there is an opportunity for the opposition to put another motion.
There is also a question with respect to the address which we are to present to Her Majesty's representative. Aside from the fact that it may well be an affront to the Governor General to leave the matter hanging the way it is, I think it is important that hon. members of this House know what the intentions of the Deputy Prime Minister are. There has been some public discussion outside this House with respect to the length of the throne speech debate, but it was always in terms of urging the government, if it was to abandon the throne speech debate, to abandon it for the purpose of bringing in a budget which would set forward the economic program of the government.

According to the Prime Minister, the reason we are here is to do something to stimulate the economy, and I hardly think that the bill which was announced, a bill to add $17 billion to the deficit of this country, is going to stimulate the economy. I think it is important that there be some understanding. Are we going to deal just with the two bills the Deputy Prime Minister announced? Have we abandoned the throne speech debate altogether?
I hope so.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
It may well be that that is the appropriate thing to do, but not without consultation.
The third question is whether we have abandoned the consultations among House leaders which have characterized the operation of this House. I regret very much to have to raise this, but I think I must because, if this place is to operate effectively and appropriately, it must operate on consultations, and not on consultations which are promised and never brought about.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret to see the hon. member in such a state of excitement. There is no intention to abandon the debate on the address in reply. It can be brought forward later, if that is the wish of the House. I had understood that there was a general desire on the part of all hon. members to proceed with the legislative program which is on the order paper. That is what I propose to do tomorrow by beginning with what I consider to be a very important economic measure. The hon. member may regard it as not important, but that is a question for debate. There will be an important economic measure proposed by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien), and it will be followed by amendments to the Old Age Security Act.
There is no intention to abandon the throne speech debate. It can be brought forward, as appropriate, and hon. members will have an opportunity to move amendments if they wish, unless there is a unanimous desire not to proceed. However, I did feel that it was appropriate at this time to interrupt the debate because we have dealt with the amendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) and the subamendment moved by the New Democratic Party. The question of confidence has been disposed of so there is no further question about that.
The hon. member referred to the matter of a meeting. I have had numerous meetings over the last several days. There have been informal contacts with members of the opposition parties. We were in consultation yesterday, and while the hon. member feels he really needed a meeting, 1 do not really think there was much necessity for a meeting to decide to proceed with these important measures.
Except that you gave your word, for what that is worth.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on the same point of order to speak on behalf of my party. I would just like to indicate to the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) that we agree with the decision to proceed with needed, important
October 18, 1978

legislation. If the Deputy Prime Minister is now saying that it is the disposition of the government to abandon the ritualistic throne speech debate, or at least substantially reduce the number of days for it, I think the people of Canada would welcome that as well as an opportunity to deal with legislation put before the House which would come to grips with the real problems which led to such an overwhelming expression of lack of confidence in this government, not simply by votes in this House, but by votes cast by the people of Canada a couple of days ago.
If the government could begin to redress that, it would certainly have our support. Let me just ask in that regard, because these things have to be worked out with the co-operation of all parties, whether the Deputy Prime Minister is saying that not only is it the government's desire to proceed with the bill he has announced for tomorrow but that it is also his understanding that, as far as the government is concerned, we will not return to the throne speech debate? If that is the government's desire, it is ours as well, but I would like to add an important proviso.
The rules provide that if we do not terminate the throne speech debate in a formal way, we cannot set up the committees of the House. That would be a serious setback to hon. members on this side of the House, who want to discuss important matters. If the Deputy Prime Minister wants to proceed now with legislation and to cut off what is largely a formality, the remainder of the throne speech debate, we are in agreement, but we insist that at the same time the government gives notice that it intends to set up the committees, which are very important, and to seek the necessary unanimous agreement of the House.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am not entirely sure that we are on safe ground on a point of order. We have discussed House business. It is the prerogative, as has been pointed out, of the government, as expressed by the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mac-Eachen), to switch off from the throne speech debate at any time, and it is not necessarily an abandonment, as he has said. What he has done and what he has announced today is in perfect order. I cannot find disorder. The subject of whether or not that is a good idea or whether the priority is right really belongs to the field of debate and is not a matter of order, and I think the matter really ought to rest there until we commence the business for tomorrow, at which time it might be the subject of debate. In the meantime, the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) patiently awaits his turn to participate in the matter before the House today.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before congratulating the mover and seconder of the address in reply I would just like to refer to a comment made by the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) a few minutes ago when he had the unparallelled audacity to suggest that the question of confidence in this government was disposed of by a vote that we had a few minutes ago. The question of confidence in this government was disposed of on Monday when people right across Canada showed how much confidence they had in the government, and if the Deputy Prime Minister wants to claim that there is confidence in the government, then he should go and advise the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to go to the people.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
This is a discredited government carrying on in a disgraceful manner after four years of their term have gone, hanging on by their fingernails, hanging on by their toenails, hanging by their handnails because they haven't got the courage to go to the Canadian people because they know what the answer is. The answer is what they got on Monday.
Let me congratulate the mover and seconder, who did an admirable job. The mover is an eloquent lady in particular. Today we had a spectacle that reminded me of Chairman Mao over in China when he said there, a few years ago, "May a hundred flowers grow". We've got 130 flowers that are withering on the other side of the House here today.
The only thing was that the 130 roses were here but the thorn was not here today-where was the Prime Minister? Is the Prime Minister so discouraged that he could not come, even though all these red roses are in the lapels of members in the House to welcome him?
Economics is a dismal science, but that science has become much more dismal in the last three or four years of this government. Is it now so dismal that one does not even like to refer to the economic statistics because the dismalness is so terrible that I do not think the people of Canada can stand much more of it.
Let us just have a quick look at what is the reason for the present economic state of Canada. Why did the Prime Minister rise in this chamber on Monday when asked a question by me about the increase in the interest rates by the central bank to 10.25 per cent, the highest increase since 1935 and the fifth increase in the last seven months, 2 per cent more than the central bank rate in the United States? The Prime Minister was asked how this corresponds with his pledge and bond to introduce a 5 per cent real growth rate in the economy, how does this correspond with the government's pledges to increase economic activity, employment and business investments in Canada. The only defence the Prime Minister has is that he is powerless, that Canada is powerless. We have a government that is powerless today to do anything to help the economic situation in Canada. When the U.S. raises its interest rates by half a percentage point, this government has to respond by

October 18, 1978
The Address-Mr. Crosbie
bouncing them up by three-quarters of a percentage point when we have already had four increases earlier this year. The government is powerless, and why? It is powerless because of its monumental incompetence in the last four or five years.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: It is a prisoner not of the law but of its total incompetence. Their past mistakes, their total economic bankruptcies, that is what they are prisoners of. Now the Prime Minister of this country, which used to be looked up to as a powerful, confident country, must get up like a beggar in the House and say he can do nothing about the most outrageous increase in interest rates in our history, except perhaps for the great depression in the early 1930s. That is the government that said the question of confidence is disposed of. Like heck it is disposed of. It will only be disposed of when this government is disposed of.

speechtext:
Look at the economic leadership of this government in the person of the lugubrious Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien). He used to be full of joy, vim, vitality, and smiles, but today he looks more sour than a prune. Who can have confidence in a minister of Finance of this government?
Here is a press clipping of June 23, 1978, from the Ottawa Journal which reads that the Minister of Finance predicts the growth for the year will be 5 per cent-"Tory member calls him Donald Duck." That was me, Mr. Speaker. He is Donald Duck because all he can do is squawk like the well-known Disney character. The minister predicted last June, only four months ago, that our economic growth rate for the year was going to be 5 per cent-that was the minister's prediction. The economists say that at best this year our growth rate will be 3.6 per cent. But the minister predicted 5 per cent. No wonder he is increasingly lugubrious, if that is the right term for the hon. gentleman. I do not know how it translates into French, but he is a lugubrious minister. The sooner he gets out, the less lugubrious the people of Canada will be.
How can you believe a word this minister says? His little shadow over there, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner), was talking about horses today. We are told that this is supposed to be the Chinese year of the horse. We thought there would be an election this year, and we would find out what end of the horse. But we have not, and the election is not coming until next year. We saw what end of this horse this is the year of today when the honourable expert on horses spoke in the question period.
The Minister of Finance predicted what our merchandise surplus was going to be this year. He predicted it was going to be $4 billion. That was on September 28. On September 29 the August trade figures came down to show our balance was only $186 million for August. The minister knew that the day before, but he misled the whole economic and financial community in Canada and in the world. The answer came the next day when he revealed surplus for August, and our dollar fell again to less than 84 cents U.S. As the right hon. member for
(Mr. Crosbie.]
Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) said, the man is a happy-go-lucky minister of finance; he thinks he has another 84 cents to go before we are finished altogether. That was bad enough, Mr. Speaker. A couple of days later the Minister of Finance said that the merchandise trade surplus would be just less than $4 billion, that it was going to be a record because the year before it was $2.9 billion. The record has changed.
What did our wonderful, lugubrious Minister of Finance say on June 1, as reported at page 5947 of Hansardl He said:
Last year we had a trade surplus of $3 billion and if the present trend goes on the surplus could reach $5 billion this year.
If he were like Pinocchio, his nose would reach right across to here. That is why the odds are so wide, not because of the wordplay but because of the noses of the ministers opposite- they are growing longer every day from the untruths they are telling the Canadian people. That is our Minister of Finance. No wonder there is no confidence.
The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce says the Canadian dollar should be worth 90 cents, that par is at 90 cents. Thank God he has left this party-it was under par when he was over here and it is over par now. According to the other side, par is at 90 cents. So I suggest we rename our Minister of Finance. Let us call him "Sink" Chretien because he sank the Canadian dollar. Here I have a heading which reads, "Chretien remarks Sink the Dollar". So we will rename the Minister of Finance "Sink" Chretien, and we will name our own finance critic John Stevens. We will then have a more accurate reflection of what is happening in Canada today. Never has a minister of finance succeeded in sinking the Canadian dollar so low. He is what we call in Newfoundland a sunker; he is just below the surface.
The Deputy Prime Minister is not here to listen to me. He might want to correct the Hansard record, correct the silly statement he made a few minutes ago about confidence. He galloped out of the House in a great hurry when he thought somebody would refer to his foolishness.
We had three ministers of finance: we had John Turner-he fled to Toronto. We had the hon. "Thumper" Macdonald-he also fled to Toronto. Toronto is the only place where the public can afford them. When will the present Minister of Finance flee to Toronto? My message to Torontonians is: arise Torontonians, you have nothing to lose but your Trudeauites. They will all go as soon as we have an election. Five went on Monday. We have had Winken, Blinken, and now we have Nod as the Minister of Finance, the three stooges of Canadian finance, the three musketeers, les miserables. We have not forgotten that the man who started it all is now in Toronto- "Blue Eyes". He is going to be black eyes if he comes out of his legal lair, I can assure him of that.
My time is limited-I do not have the time to really let go here.

I will only refer to one forecast because I cannot stand to refer to any more. Woods, Gordon, a well-
October 18, 1978

known Liberal firm, made a forecast and said that next year we will have a decline in housing starts, a decline in auto sales, an unemployment rate of 9.2 per cent, an inflation rate of 8.3 per cent, and a real growth rate of only 2.5 per cent. There is a glowing introduction to the election year by that Liberal firm. At least they speak the truth. There is a forecast from a firm which you could expect to be on the conservative side when estimating what might happen next year. So next year will be worse than the years we have just gone through.
What this country needs and what our economy needs is a complete purge, a complete laxative. They need to be purged of this government, to have a complete cleanout. That is the only way to get our economic system working again because we have no confidence whatsoever in this government. The Minister of Finance is hopeless, hopeless, hopeless. He is the minister of Nod.
What about the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce? He is the next strong man in the government in economic affairs. What is his prediction? Last May 12 he was reported in the Winnipeg Tribune to have stated that "by fall it will be obvious that the economy will pick up a great deal." It is not so obvious to the rest of the people in Canada. We are now in the fall. What did he say on November 9, 1977, in Winnipeg? He said that the fall of the dollar was useful. Well, I suppose he is delighted now that it is down to 84 cents.
Also on November 9, 1977, he stated that we are on the threshold of tremendous growth. That was the prediction of this mighty economic czar who sits in the hallowed halls or the glass halls where once the mighty Howe sat. From Howe to Horner is a purge, all right. He said just last fall that we were on the threshold of tremendous growth. In May he said that it is obvious the economy is picking up a great deal since the fall. On October 5 he stated in Sarnia that the Canadian economy is entering a period of stable growth.
Now, there is something wrong there. It is picking up in one place, it is booming tremendously and on the threshold of tremendous growth, and now it is entering a period of stable growth.

Yes, that is because the minister is an expert on horses. That is where he got the idea that we are into a period of stable growth.
What did he say in the House on Friday, October 13, bad luck day? It was "Bad Day at Black Rock" for the Canadian dollar, interest rates, investments, householders, mortgage holders and borrowers. He said:
-one thing is clear in this debate and will probably run through the entire thirtieth parliament, and that is that we have a healthy economy and a strong, confident private sector in our country.
Honestly, ladies and gentlemen of the House of Commons, can you believe it, that the minister said we have a healthy economy and a strong confident private sector in our country? We hardly have a man in the private sector who has not got his
The Address-Mr. Crosbie
fingernails bitten down to his toenails, he is so confident about what this government has done for him! He admitted, though, on the same page, that while unemployment and inflation are still too high, Canada is working its way through the difficult world economic problems better than most countries. What countries, Mr. Speaker? Zanzibar, Zambia? The Kwacha is still a bit stronger than the Canadian dollar. Nepal? Where are these countries? Malawi, Malagasy? What countries are doing so much better than Canada? Who does he think will swallow this kind of material?
On August 1 the Prime Minister realized something was wrong. He has only been here ten years. It took him ten years to realize that something was wrong. He came back from Morocco. He is better than Bob Hope on "The road to Morocco." He went on television and announced a whole new series of programs which contradicted, violated, and raped all the earlier programs, principles and practices of the government. From restraint to you-know-what, he changed and reversed. His ministers heard about it for the first time on television. That was just as well. They could not have understood, anyway. The commentators said that what the Prime Minister was starting was a political striptease. The Minister of Finance came out, had a press conference, and he stripped. The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) came out and he stripped. Some other minister came out and he stripped. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce was sent to Japan. We do not know what he did there. Probably he stripped. But anyway, they all came out and stripped, these ministers did. It was a political striptease. When they were finished with their strip, what did the Canadian public see? They saw that underneath the government's clothes there was nothing but falsies. That is why we have had such a result in the by-elections.
We have to look on the bright side of this thing. At least we can joke about the government. But I know it is no joking matter. Before passing on, although time is pressing, I should like to give a considered opinion which I read some time ago. It is by Mr. John Turner. He said that the political interregnum which Canada now faces is deepening, with the resulting increase in economic hazards. If their friends are giving such candid opinions about them, what must their enemies be saying? I declare myself a friend of the government by what I am saying openly here today. One does not have to pay a cent to hear it. He gets it all for free. By the way, it is two years since the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mrs. Pigott) and I joined the hallowed ranks in these halls.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

Every time I have spoken here I thought it was the last time. I thought that the big, brave government was going to call the election, and every time was not the last time. Here I am again ready for another eight months of howling and bawling.

-one cannot rule out a full crisis of confidence in the Canadian dollar.

The Address-Mr. Crosbie We certainly cannot. It continues:
Unfortunately, there is also weakness in some key economic ministries of the federal government. In Finance, as already noted, the minister has been seriously hurt.
That is for sure. We see that every day in the lugubrious look on the minister's face. He is badly hurt. On page 10 Mr. Turner is quoted as saying the following:
-Jack Horner is effectively spending 95 per cent of his time away from the job on his re-election problems.
He can spend 100 per cent of his time away and he will not cure that problem. It continues:
This leaves him a totally inadequate amount of time to learn and cope with his job, which is evident from a succession of reports on his performance.
High praise indeed from one of his friends in the Liberal party. I can see that leadership convention now. I wonder who brother Horner will support.
He goes on to say:
Finally, in Energy, Mines and Resources, the minister is generally perceived to lack the confidence of the Prime Minister.
The Prime Minister is an intelligent man. He agrees with all the rest of us. He lacks our confidence. This is the verdict of their friends on their performance. One of their own friends is waiting in Toronto now for the call.
Let me get down to some other problems. There is chaos in this government of policy. I should like to refer to the government of Newfoundland as an example. They talk about restraint. The Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council this afternoon had the gall to mention restraint. The government announced a few weeks ago that it was going to transfer most of the personnel from the Gander weather office to Halifax. The government was going to cut back on meteorological spending. It does not like forecasts any more, weather forecasts, political forecasts, or any kind of forecasts. It is going to save a few hundred thousand dollars. Now that has been reversed.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson), who is now in Namibia, is an expert on Namibia. A couple of months ago he thought Namibia was an item of babies' clothes. Now he is down in South Africa solving the problems of Namibia. He made an announcement on October 4. I spoke to the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc) in the afternoon at five o'clock and he told me that the station was crazy, Gander should be shut, everything should go to Halifax, and that it is all done on computers. On that night at ten o'clock the Secretary of State for External Affairs announced that Newfoundland is all cancelled. That is why the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment has not been around. It is the first time that we scalped one of them. The Secretary of State for External Affairs scalped the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment. At ten o'clock he announced that this decision was reversed, even though the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment had told me a few hours earlier that it was still in effect. That is what is called chaos.

What else happened? I should like to refer to an article entitled "Ultimatum to Trudeau, Hands Off Gander" which appeared in The Daily News on October 4, 1978. In part it reads as follows:
George Baker, MP for Gander-Twillingate, threatened to bolt the Liberal party unless the federal government changed its mind about downgrading the Gander weather office-
That is what it is now, government by bolt. The decision depends on who is going to bolt next. The hon. member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker) said that he was going to bolt. This government which is so hot now about restraint and twittering about restraint, changed its mind and announced a decision without the concurrence of the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment. The announcement was just made. It was telephoned from Ottawa down to Newfoundland. I will bet any amount that the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment knew nothing about that announcement. This is not government, this is chaos.
The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce has had an application from Newfoundland since March for a synchrolift to be installed in the government-owned dockyard in St. John's. It is paying them some eight million lousy dollars for a synchrolift which will give 200 jobs and put the yard in the position of handling 60 Russian trawlers a year. We have been waiting sinch March. Why? We have been waiting because the Secretary of State for External Affairs was up here skulking around and sabotaging it because there is a shipyard in his own district, and the people in his district mistakenly think that the dry dockyard in St. John's, if it gets this synchrolift, is going to compete with them or do something to harm them. That is not true at all, but they think it is true. The minister skulked around and made an announcement in Newfoundland. I am looking for the clipping.
By the way, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce said in this House, as reported in The Telegram on April 20, that the federal government is going to make substantive expenditures to upgrade our dockyards. That is what he told the House finance committee, that it was now in the midst of negotiations. He said that the decision should be reached in a matter of weeks rather than months. They are cowering in that department, afraid of the Secretary of State for External Affairs because he barked at them. What did he bark? He went down to Newfoundland, the Secretary of State for External Affairs did, and he made a statement down there. What was his statement? Where is that statement? He has made a lot of statements down there. I know I should not have had all these bloody clippings together. What he said, Mr. Speaker, was-I knew that I should not have had all these bloody clippings together. What he said was this; that you are only going to get a synchrolift in the dockyard in St. John's, which we own, to give you 200 jobs and save the 300 there if you are able to prove-yes, here it is.

speechtext:
The city has to prove that the lift will not hurt Marystown. This is the St. John's dockyard in Newfoundland which employs 300 Newfoundlanders and could employ 200 more and it has to prove if it gets a synchrolift that it will not hurt a shipyard in Marystown. What about Halifax? Do we have to prove that we will not hurt Halifax, that we will not hurt Quebec, or that we will not hurt Esquimalt?
There have been seven shipyards across Canada that have received assistance from the government this year, and none of them had to prove that they would not hurt St. John's or Marystown. But this "bully boy" makes the announcement in St. John's on September 13 that we cannot have a synchrolift unless we can prove it will not hurt Marystown in his district. Do you know, Mr. Speaker, that the minister did not even know about it? I spent two weeks calling the minister. You talk about courtesy; I never even got a call back from him, and I am the critic for industry, trade and commerce and a member of this House. When I was a minister I called back any member who called me, immediately. For two weeks I did not get an answer back from that minister until finally I got a call from his secretary telling me not to worry, that everything was in good hands, everything was under control. I said to one of his executive assistants-he has a plethora of them-"Do you realize that Mr. Jamieson just two weeks ago gave the death knell to this and it is not going to St. John's unless we can prove that it will not hurt Marystown? How can we prove that negative?" He said, "No, he hadn't heard that."
Who is making the policies for this government, Mr. Speaker? This is not a government, it is a collection of "whirlygigs", pushers, and pressure pumpers. And whoever has the biggest pressure pump is apparently running every department. I spoke to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce yesterday and he promised me that everything is in good hands, everything is hunky-dory, and that everything is going to be favourable, that he is going to announce it when he gets to Newfoundland some day. We will give him a great welcome, but I am announcing it now. If we can entice the minister down to Newfoundland, he will announce it, but only if the Secretary of State for External Affairs allows him. He has to get the permission of the Secretary of State for External Affairs who is in Namibia at the moment, the same gentleman who went on a trip last year to the Middle East.
I have a report from the Journal dated November 8, 1977, with the headline, "If Nothing Else We Have King Tut," which says that he visited all the countries of the Middle East. At the conclusion of the trip in Cairo the Minister said:
There's a flexibility which I perceived here with regard to a formula under which talks may be resolved and a general disposition to look with an open mind on a wide range of issues.
I do not know what he meant, nor does anybody else. He goes on to say that he:
-arrived in Spain during a four-day holiday weekend and in Greece during an election campaign and a torrential storm in which 25 people died. These tended to distract his hosts.
The Address-Mr. Crosbie
I hope the results of the minister's trip to South Africa are just as harmless as his trip to the Middle East last fall. I am prepared to fight that gentleman, tooth and nail, until he comes across with my synchrolift.
What has happened in unemployment insurance? A despicable change in the law was announced that is going to crucify the seasonally employed in Newfoundland and the maritime provinces. One of the Liberal backbenchers, the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Rompkey) was quoted in the paper as threatening revolt by the Atlantic Liberal backbenchers if these changes that discriminated against the seasonally employed went through. The minister has caved in, and it is a good thing that he did because the revolt is nothing compared with what he would get from this side if he had not made some changes.
That is the government today, Mr. Speaker; they make a decision one day and reverse it the next. That was the Romp-key revolt. We have had the Baker revolt, and the Jamieson revolt. The whole thing is revolting; the government is revolting. It is not a government, it is a revolving, poll-taking machine. The left hand does not know what the left hand is doing. It is dancing in the dark, the old Cole Porter tune which should be the cabinet theme song.
In my last couple of minutes, Mr. Speaker, let me refer quickly to the Newfoundland railway. This is another thing that the Secretary of State for External Affairs talked about in Newfoundland on September 12. He made the announcement. His announcement was that the Government of Canada was not going to accept the recommendation by the royal commission that the Newfoundland railway be phased out, because everyone in Newfoundland, with the exception of our candidate in Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe, had said that the railway should stay. The one man in Newfoundland who said that the railway should go had an unfortunate occurrence in the by-elections.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) did not appear to know that the Secretary of State for External Affairs had already said that the Canadian government would not accept the recommendation. Now they are laying off employees, taking certain trains off the schedule, and laying 20 men off at the end of this month, despite the minister's commitment made in March of 1977 that there would be no lay-offs or changes in service while that royal commission was in effect.
Yesterday the minister in this House gave a weasel-worded answer to my question which completely changed his commitment. It was "baffle-gab" of the worst kind. He said that there could be lay-offs of a seasonal load-related nature throughout the system. I will tell him where the load-related nature of the system is; it is right here at the top. We are sick of these kinds of loads. He is putting this on the backs of the railway workers in Newfoundland. I do not have time to develop the situation further today.

October 18, 1978
The Address-Mr. Crosbie
We have a $17 billion borrowing bill coming up tomorrow. We cannot go on with the address in reply because the government want the authority to borrow another $17 billion for their bungling. I am going to debate every cent of those billions, and I hope that nobody tells me that it is an emergency to give this crowd another $17 billion tomorrow. It is not an economic program, is it, Mr. House leader?
I have to shorten this up, Mr. Speaker, because we are allowed only 30 minutes. I am used to 90 as a minimum, which was what we had in the Newfoundland house, or usually it was unlimited. I would like to make an amendment and move that the following be added to the address:
but this House regrets to inform Your Excellency that the policies of your ministers have severely damaged the Canadian economy, and that your ministers have not proposed those measures of taxation relief, including home mortgage interest and property tax deductibility, which would promote economic growth and recovery and ensure a more equitable tax system for all Canadians.
I move this, seconded by the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker), in the full realization, which is selfobvious, that the ministers have severely damaged our economy, that they have not proposed taxation relief, and in the hope that the gentlemen to my left here will come to their senses and help rescue the middle and lower income people of Canada who have a home now or who want to get one, who want to borrow under a mortgage and who want relief from the effects of the stupid actions of this government. These people are being crucified with an 11 Vi per cent mortgage rate, and when they go to the banks they are going to be stuck with a rate of 11V4 or 12 per cent.
We want to rescue these people from the Liberal excesses which have put them in this position. We want to open up home ownership for more people in Canada. This is a program that is going to help sweep this government opposite out of power, because when something was proposed which makes some sense and which the people want, instead of adopting it for the next budget, as they usually do they spoke against it. Even a boa constrictor could not twist itself around enough to include this great proposal in the next Liberal budget. They cannot do that any longer. Even the lugubrious Minister of Finance would not have the gall or the audacity to try to slip around the statements he has made in the past few weeks to bring in a budget that contained this great new principle, which we are going to introduce as soon as we get back from the electorate and the election of 1979.
Is my time up, Mr. Speaker, or do I have another minute or two?

speechtext:
I must confess, Mr. Speaker, I had not realized that. This is fantastic. It is like an early Christmas. Now, where was I? What joy!
I shall go back to the railway, Mr. Speaker. When the royal commission was set up on March 28, 1977, the Minister of

Transport was down in St. John's. He had a press conference aboard a coastguard vessel, and it is lucky for him that it was tied to the wharf so that he did not get seasick. I would like to read some of what the minister said which was quoted in the St. John's Evening Telegram of March 29, 1977. The minister said that that study:
-won't be just another study to lie on the shelf because the province is ''at a critical point" for decisions, Transport Minister Otto Lang yesterday maintained. "I consider this one the final one"-
It's the final one for him all right.
-he said following a press conference in St. John's, for "we cannot wait any longer for tough decisions . .. and good decisions for Newfoundland."
That was his statement. He went on in the interview to say that:
-he has asked CN not to proceed with any technological or structural changes during the course of the study that would "disadvantageously affect" employment.
These are pretty peculiar words, but everybody in Newfoundland understood them to mean there would not be any lay-offs as a result while this royal commission was under way. Imagine him saying that in Newfoundland-you would not "disadvantageously affect employment". That might go over in Saskatchewan but we do not think much of it in Newfoundland. He said there would be no lay-offs.
I have another clipping here to show what is going on now. The commission made an interim report last June, which was published by the government somewhere around July 20. I announced it first, by the way. Two days earlier I announced the royal commission's conclusions and came out against them, the first one in that province to come out against the abandonment of our railway. The minister confirmed what I had to say, two days later. He was a bit late in releasing the report.
A heading in a newspaper article of October 14 reads:
Rail Union Plans Strong Protest Against Lay-offs
It says they eliminated two trains in a decision made in Moncton and St. John's and that 20 people would be laid off. That is how much the minister's word is worth.
Yesterday he said in his pallid way that he was going to investigate that. Let me give you the full effect of what he said, now that I have the time, and because it is so shocking in its transparent mendacity that I can hardly contain myself. When I asked him yesterday about these lay-offs this is what he said, as reported in Hansard at page 164:
Mr. Speaker, rather more exactly the instruction was that there would be no lay-offs during the course of the commission except those which were related to changes in the level and flow of business of the ordinary sort because, of course, there are lay-offs of a seasonal and load-related nature throughout the system.
That is pretty clear, Mr. Speaker. He has made it clear that Dr. Bandeen's commission's work will end in January. He continued:
I would be glad to investigate whether a specific lay-off is under the exceptional category which may be permitted or is of such significance that it actually contravenes the understanding.
The minister has not reported to me yet.
October 18, 1978

I will tell you what will happen to the minister if he comes down there and gives us his "seasonal and load-related nature" of the system. We will take the system and wrap it around his neck and drop him off the dock at Port-aux-Basques. How could the minister say that when he has made a promise to the 3,000 railway workers in Newfoundland that there would be no lay-offs while this royal commission did its work? He is not here now to listen to me, and, it would not do any good if he were. He also said, as I quoted a few minutes ago, that this was going to be the "last commission", "critical point", and mentioned "good tough decisions".
One of the recommendations in the interim report of that commission was that the CN bus system in Newfoundland was beyond contempt. Their finding was that the buses were beyond description and there was poor service. In July of 1976, in the course of federal-provincial relations, the Minister of Transport took the CN bus system that was established in Newfoundland to replace our lost railway passenger service- it was under the Public Utilities Commission of Newfoundland who were regulating it satisfactorily-he took it from them and put it under the Canadian Transport Commission. Since that time they were allowed an 8 per cent fare increase in 1976, and 15 per cent in 1977. CN applied to the CTC. They had a hearing at the beginning of November. The CTC allowed them to put the fare increase they asked for into effect as an interim increase of 15 per cent, and said they would give a final decision later. They gave the final decision in August this summer, eight or nine months later. Imagine a regulatory body doing that. They allowed what was asked for, a 15 per cent increase in the interim, and the interim period was eight months or nine months. Then they brought down the report to confirm the 15 per cent was all right.
The CN has the ball, and what do you think the CN did? Did they think they were lucky to get that in such a slippery manner? The CN came in two weeks later and applied for another 36 per cent increase, to go into effect in November of this fall and in February next.
I wrote the minister on August 3. I wish he would read his mail. I am always getting little notes from some assistant saying the minister is going to respond in due course. He has not responded yet. "Due course" has not arrived. I wrote on August 3 and pointed out that the Sullivan Commission-the minister's commission, had this to say at page 127:
The CN Roadcruiser service has been operating with old, unsuitable, totally inadquate equipment. The bus is satisfactory for short distance travel, but for long trips is unacceptable as a replacement for the train. From a level of service standpoint, and in light of the concessions made to train travel in other provinces, CN fares are far and above what is reasonable.
That is a devastating indictment of this roadcruiser service. I pointed out to the minister that at page 245 of its report the commission stated that the roadcruiser operation is an equal substitution for the rail passenger service, and that fares must remain at a level lower than similar fares which might be payable for similar distances on a trans-island train service.
The Address-Mr. Crosbie
The commission report went to say:
Certainly, no increase in fares must be permitted until substantial improvements are made in the facilities being offered on the corridor at present.
The commission suggested that the federal government give the same subsidy for this service as they give for other passenger service in the other nine provinces of Canada.
The Canadian National, this crown corporation, this creature of the government, after receiving that report and after getting a 15 per cent increase confirmed, and eight year before, came back for 36 per cent.
The Newfoundland government has protested, the people of Newfoundland have protested, I have protested, as has the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), and we cannot get an answer. This government has got to direct the CN-"No increase." Why was the minister saying, when this commission was established, that it would be given every consideration, that decisions had to be made, and then make a report on the CN bus service in Newfoundland crucifying the bus passengers? They want a 36 per cent increase! This minister now has to direct them-"No increase." Never mind the Canadian Transport Commission. We have no regard for the Canadian Transport Commission in Newfoundland. We think it is a hopeless body. It is a tool of the vested interest, a tool of the crown corporation. We have no faith or trust in it. The minister has to reverse this decision and act on the recommendations of that royal commission.
The railway, which has been allowed to run down, is owned by the Government of Canada. It has been given to CN to operate. CN has been losing money on it. CN does not want to put any more of its own revenues or profits from some other part of Canada into the Newfoundland service. We can understand that. The royal commission made a recommendation that it should close. The CN is losing $20 or $30 million a year on this service.
The government has made the decision now to close the Newfoundland railway, and it should not. Why should we be deprived of the rail mode of transportation in Newfoundland? The government has to make up the losses that are properly found each year by the right body, to the CN But the government will not do that. CN is knifing our railway to death. They are determined to kill it within the next 12 months because they will not realize their responsibilities. CN cannot be expected to subsidize the Newfoundland railway from its other railways and other services across Canada. Only government can do that. They have to direct CN. to make an honest effort to operate this railway.
Three thousand people in Newfoundland work for that railway, Mr. Speaker, with all that entails for Newfoundland. Every responsible body, and irresponsible body, has come out to say that it has to continue and we do not want it to stop. It is a mode of transportation and we have to continue that option in Newfoundland. The government is doing nothing, despite telegrams and wires from the Newfoundland government. They have ignored it, Mr. Speaker. They will not meet with the railway unions. The minister will not meet with me.

October 18, 1978
The Address-Mr. Gray
He will not meet with the Newfoundland government. I do not know who he is meeting with. He has too many portfolios.
Transport would kill any ordinary man or woman, yet that minister is given the wheat board, and justice-everything is sloughed off on him, and he is equally obnoxious in every one of them but particularly so in transportation. He is not a superman; none of us are supermen. I have every sympathy for the huge burden he has in transportation, but I lose my sympathy when we try to deal with him in any human situation at all.
They talk about federal-provincial relations. I am going to give you a story, Mr. Speaker, about the federal-provincial relations and about the problems. I had to laugh when the Prime Minister came on television on August 1. He had the audacity to come on TV and say hello to the Queen and how glad he was that she had arrived in Canada. He was not even there when she arrived in Newfoundland, Mr. Speaker, to meet her. He was in Morocco concocting his TV address for a couple of days later.
We believe in the British connection in Newfoundland, Mr. Speaker, and in our relationship with the Queen and her continuance as Queen of the Commonwealth and her relationship to us in all of Canada. We agree with Senator Forsey and his criticism of the constitutional proposals, which are now going to be changed-the attempt to change all of that. It is just symbolic anyway-another evidence of our history.
In that connection, Mr. Speaker, the government of Newfoundland wrote-
