speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) spoke to the country last August he announced the federal government would be giving a new and higher priority to dealing with the country's economic problems. I have been among those calling on the government to establish such a priority in the light of our still too high unemployment and the resulting need for more economic growth in Canada. I have also been calling on the government to take prompt action in developing and implementing programs to deal effectively with these kinds of problems.
I welcome this new and higher priority which is confirmed in the throne speech. The speech also confirms the kinds of programs the government has in mind to carry out this priority. The Speech from the Throne says, as did the Prime Minister earlier, that the government would greatly reduce its expenditures leaving more room to the private sector, and in this way help it to grow and flourish. It says the government will make changes in its programs to help revive the economy through greater private sector activity. The speech also proposes further changes in the unemployment insurance system to remove disincentives to work, as well as the taking of steps
[Mr. Crosbie.)
to provide more help to senior citizens and other low income Canadians hurt most by continuing inflationary pressures. But in spite of statements we have had from various ministers, I believe there is still a need for more detailed information about the government's proposals so that informed judgments can be made about their real impact on the country.
This throne speech opens a new session of parliament. This means the parliamentary process will be in operation to help get out the necessary information and to enable the merits of the government's proposals implementing its new economic program to be considered in some depth. Also this process will be a vehicle for making changes to those parts of this program which may, in fact, be in conflict with its objectives, or have unintended negative side effects for the country's social or economic fabric.
Canadians are understandably concerned about the levels government expenditures have been reaching because of what this means in terms of such things as the level of taxation, government borrowing, deficits and so on. But if the federal government simply makes cuts in its expenditures and does not balance these cuts with equivalent expenditure in other areas or with equivalent cuts in taxes, or both, the result surely will be to hold back the economy, to restrain its growth, rather than aid in its recovery. This is because the government will be spending less than before, but taking the same amount out of the economy.
One hears many comments to the effect that government spending has been holding back the economy. However, this spending is for goods and services it buys from the private sector. Or it is, to a much greater extent, in the form of transfer payments to individuals who use them as income to buy such goods and services, or also for transfer payments to other levels of government which spend them for these purposes. Therefore a reduction in federal government expenditure by itself is simply a reduction in total demand in the economy. To avoid being a restraint on it, this reduction, in my view, has to be matched with tax cuts, or at least, as an alternative, the money saved from cuts in spending in some areas has to be reallocated in ways that are hopefully more effective in encouraging more sound, private economic activity. It should be noted though that some economists argue that if this is done the effect on the economy would simply be neutral.
So far the government has not announced a re-allocation of expenditure equal to the reductions which have also been announced. And while the Prime Minister said in his speech in August that there would be tax cuts, the government as yet has not announced any program of reductions in personal or corporate taxes to help balance the reductions in government expenditure that have already been put forward.
However, I am pleased that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) now says he intends to present a budget in mid-November. In my view, this budget must be the instrument for putting in place at an early date a balanced program made up of personal tax cuts and economic incentive measures for business where justified and required, as well as government
October 18, 1978

programs for public investment and direct employment to back up these other measures.
The throne speech says a proposal will be placed before the House "to provide for the review by parliament of evaluations by the government of major programs." Something along these lines should be brought forward very early in this new session. Even if one agrees with the need to cut government expenditures, it is possible to have valid concerns about the way these reductions are being carried out, about whether wise choices are being made about the programs to be reduced or eliminated.
We know generally what programs the government intends to eliminate or reduce. However, even here in many cases officials are still unable to provide a full and detailed picture of exactly what is being done. Neither parliament nor the public has been informed of the alternatives the government considered and rejected in place of the cuts it announced, and the exact reasons why these particular cuts were selected.
There is no provision for input from parliament and the public in the expenditure-review process at a point before the government is locked into a particular decision arising from it. Therefore, as a result, it is difficult to bring about changes in such decisions without some form of confrontation between some portions of the community and the government over a particular program expenditure reduction. But even these confrontations take place without having information to start with as to why the government made that decision, and without a meaningful opportunity to present views and alternatives to it.
One approach in dealing with the concern would be to have an appropriate parliamentary committee begin hearings as soon as possible after this throne speech debate is over. They would be on the government expenditure cuts in programs that have been announced, and the committee would hear evidence as to why a particular cut was decided on. Also what the alternatives may be, if any, which would still enable the same over-all expenditure reduction target to be achieved.
Such a committee could examine, for example, whether in fact bureaucratic structures are being maintained while reductions are being made in programs that provide needed information and service to the public. For instance, the Department of the Environment could explain why cutting out regional offices would not be a preferred alternative to eliminating the Petawawa Forest Research Station, the fisheries research laboratories in Nova Scotia, and weather ships off the coast of British Columbia. The committee could examine allegations that the Treasury Board and the Department of Finance are not making any meaningful cuts at all in their own bureaucratic structures. The committee could examine whether it is valid for the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs to reduce the number of inspections presently being carried out in the field to ensure that hazardous products and food products of questionable quality are not being offered to Canadian consumers, or whether it is correct for the department to be reducing its direct consumer complaint handling services, all in place of other kinds of cuts.
The Address-Mr. Gray
The government says its intention in changing the unemployment insurance system is to move away from simply providing income payments toward using these funds to ensure that unemployed people get training to provide them with skills they lack to fill available jobs. Therefore the committee could inquire why, if this is the case, the government at the same time apparently has under way a serious reduction in existing funding to provide training allowances to these people.
It would appear that the proposed changes in the unemployment insurance system could mean that as many as several hundred thousand Canadians would not be eligible for payments from it in the way they are at present. If there are not, in fact, jobs available for them which are not now being filled, either because of disincentives to work in the present system or, as may be likely, flaws in its administration, these people will simply be thrown on to municipal and provincial welfare rolls. This will mean that the total public expenditure presently involved will continue but will come, to a much greater extent than before, out of municipal and provincial taxes rather than from federal government funds. This means that in many parts of the country the burden will shift to levels of government with a tax base smaller and less equitable than the one available to the federal government. There will be no saving in terms of total public expenditures. It will simply shift to levels of government less able to assume it. This could be a very serious matter for large areas of the country like the Atlantic provinces.
I am pleased to note the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) has some of these aspects under review because of representations by members of the Liberal caucus from the Atlantic provinces and similar areas.
It would appear, however, that only a relatively limited amount of the money the federal government hopes to save through its proposed changes in the unemployment insurance system has been allocated so far to expanding its employment strategy programs, its programs for job creation, beyond what was intended to be spent by the government before it decided to propose the changes in the unemployment insurance system in question. If more funds are not reallocated, this could have unfortunate consequences for a substantial number of individual Canadians and their families everywhere in Canada, even those in regions like Ontario.
Up to this point I have not seen enough detailed information to confirm to me that there will be the necessary high level of co-ordination in the Department of Employment and Immigration to ensure that for all those who will no longer be eligible for unemployment insurance when the proposed changes go into effect, and who are ready and willing to work, there will be either a job at reasonable wages and working conditions, or skill training to help them qualify for those jobs that are available. Nor does the information I have seen so far confirm there will be the necessary co-ordination and effort in the department to ensure that as a last resort some form of

October 18, 1978
The Address-Mr. Gray
meaningful direct employment under government auspices will be available for all of these people.
Much has been said about how the kinds of steps announced by the Prime Minister and certain of his ministers in recent weeks will help restore "business confidence" and that this is what is required in order to get business to increase its investment to expand its activity in Canada. However, it seems to me that business confidence means confidence that it can and will earn a reasonable profit from its activities. Surely this means having sufficient numbers of people in Canada with the level of income needed to buy goods and services produced by business at prices that will yield these kinds of profits. Businessmen are hardly likely to have the necessary kind of confidence if government policy turns out to reduce rather than to maintain and expand the necessary spending power of individual Canadians and their families. Of course it is also argued that business confidence is being inhibited by excessive government involvement in the market place and in the economy generally.
In considering this issue I think it is necessary to look carefully at all aspects of it and to define what is being talked about and what is meant when one speaks of excessive government involvement in the economy. In my view, and I think there is wide agreement on this, the government should always be striving to be more efficient in all its activities and to lessen dramatically burdens of bureaucracy and red tape. It is certainly my objective to have the government operate generally in a more efficient, effective, and competent manner. It does not follow, however, that any particular activity by government is not important and necessary for the well-being both of business and the consumer simply because a valid argument can be made for improving the way the government administers that activity.
Frankly, I do not think that we would have any kind of enterprise system or market system at all today without much of the government involvement in it that has developed over the past 50 years or so. After all, that market system, when left entirely to its own devices, brought the stock market crash of 1929 and the deep-seated depression of the 1930s that followed. These, in turn, helped to cause the public at large to demand of governments in North America and the western world the development of present-day programs which stabilize the economy and maintain incomes, and which have helped prevent a recurrence, if not of all economic slumps, at least of much of the misery associated with them 40 years ago.
The unlimited, uncontrolled operation of the market system 50 or more years ago, and the unsafe working conditions that were general in it, as well as the dangerous products freely sold through its operation, helped cause the public to demand that government institute the programs to set basic standards for health and safety that we have today. The public also demanded the creation of programs now providing basic standards of income for our older or less fortunate citizens.
The ability of some unscrupulous operators in the market place to drive out competitors and dominate it through monopoly and combines for their benefit, led the public,

including many in business, to urge government to set up ground rules for competition through anti-trust or competition legislation.
As I have said, it is possible for government involvement in the market place to be excessive and heavy-handed and we have to guard against this and work to prevent it. However, at the same time, without forms of government involvement to provide a framework and set basic standards on behalf of the community at large, there would likely be no market system at all, with the opportunities it provides for private initiative in Canada and our western society today. Instead, the bulk of the population seeing only the actual and potential abuses of a market system left entirely to its own devices would long ago have supported one or the other of the forms of totalitarianism of the right or the left we now see in all too many of the other parts of the world.
Of course there is a great deal of ambivalence even on the part of those who profess to be the strongest protagonists of free enterprise on the issue of government involvement in the economy.
No business voice in my own Windsor area objected to the decision of the federal and provincial governments to give a grant of $68 million to Ford Motor Company to get it to locate its new engine plant in that area. This grant came about at the initiative of the federal government which provided the larger part of the funds. When the grant was announced, it was looked on, and correctly in my view, as a form of investment with returns to the public through taxes to all three levels of government, through more than two and a half thousand jobs directly created by the operation of the new plant, and through further spill-over economic activity benefiting all of Canada, returns being many times greater than the total grant over only a few years time.
Also, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) announced a few weeks ago that a further $300 million had been set aside by the government to support, through grants or loans, further innovative business activity. When he did this, no spokesmen of the business community got up and said, "No, keep the money, we don't want it, this should not be done by the federal government; just decrease government expenditure by this amount." But this $300 million program is a form of federal government involvement in the economy, one which will hopefully turn out to be most worth-while for Canadians generally.
At the same time I hope this program will not turn out to be simply an exercise in providing funds in an ad hoc and reactive manner. Instead, the government should move promptly to put in place an industrial strategy for Canada with this program as one of its key elements. I and others have spoken about the need for such a strategy which would mean a new kind of coherent, intergrated set of federal programs to encourage a stronger and larger industrial sector in Canada, one which is more comptetitive and innovative in meeting the challenges of both domestic and world markets.
The government has had for some weeks the reports of the 24 industry sector task forces set up earlier this year. These
October 18, 1978

can provide useful information and suggestions for components of an industrial strategy. However, each report appears to discuss matters from the special perspective of people from the industry it deals with. It is the responsibility of the government to make decisions as to the best ideas which could be taken from each of these studies and from other work, like that of the Science Council, as well.
It is the responsibility of the government to reach conclusions, to make decisions, as to which industrial sectors in Canada are most likely to be winners in domestic and world markets and therefore deserving of additional if not new kinds of federal government support because of the potential of those sectors, regardless of their regional location or their present health. These are the kinds of decisions by government which are urgently required if we are finally to put in place the integrated industrial strategy necessary, if we are to provide additional jobs and improve standards of living for our growing labour force. Such a strategy is needed to eliminate or, at least, to reverse the trend to deindustrialization, the decrease in industrial activity and the decline in the number of industrial jobs in Canada which are all too frighteningly evident if one looks at statistics showing the relatively low percentage of our exports which are in the form of finished manufactured goods.
I return to the matter of government involvement in the economy. Hon. members may recall that a month or so ago three school buses involved in an accident near Hamilton were found to be in an unsafe condition. It was disclosed that the Ontario provincial government had been allowing the company owning these buses to inspect them itself and to put government safety stickers on them. A high proportion of the entire bus fleet was found not to meet provincial government safety standards. I am sure that even strong proponents of deregulation and of eliminating government involvement in the economy were quite happy, especially if their own children were riding those buses, to see the Ontario government finally tighten up its procedures and increase the number and extent of its own bus safety inspections.
This bus safety incident illustrates the limitations of selfregulation by business in the absence of, at the very least, some form of effective monitoring by government. It could be an invitation to abuse by the unscrupulous. It could allow the creation of pressures, in line with the understandable objective of maximizing profit, which could encourage even the well intentioned to cut corners in ways contrary to the best interests of the public. Thus, in my view, there is a continuing need for forms of regulation by government on behalf of the community at large to ensure that all who come together in the market place will get a fair deal there and circumstances where their health and safety are protected.
I regret, therefore, the absence of any specific mention in the Speech from the Throne of a commitment by the government to attempt, at least, to have implemented in this session the second and final stage of the much needed reform and updating of competition policy. I also regret the absence of any
The Address-Mr. Gray
indication in the speech of a similar commitment to implementing borrowers' and depositors' protection legislation. The government itself made a case for these measures very well in its own white paper "Agenda For Co-operation" and I would urge the government to move, for the reasons the government itself has given, to have these measures adopted by parliament in the current session. Their purpose is to set reasonable ground rules for the fair and efficient operation of the market place and not to hamper that kind of operation. These measures are therefore quite consistent with the government's current approach of relying to an increased extent on private sector activity for economic recovery.
I speak today, as always, in a constructive sense as one who wants to see the government operate in such a way that the public will give it majority support in the next general election. If the government demonstrates in the course of the present session that it can deal effectively with matters of real concern and importance to individual Canadians and their families, particularly as consumers, workers, and small business people, I believe it can and will win that majority support when the election comes.
But there is one more thing I want to talk about today. Although the government's new higher priority for dealing with economic issues is welcome, the national unity issue remains important. The issues of the economy and of national unity remain closely intertwined. Without unity we shall not be able to deal with our economic problems and unless we deal effectively with those problems we shall not be able to maintain our unity. This means that constitutional reform continues to require attention. Improving the economy and making decisions on constitutional change are both necessary in order to ensure that the majority of Quebeckers continue to wish to be part of Canada. Both are necessary if we are to respond to views expressed in all regions of Canada that improvements in our present constitutional set-up and in the general format of government operations are needed in order that the framework upon which all activity, whether economic or social in our country is based, may be better and more effective.
This must not mean, however, that Canada would no longer have a strong central government, a national government, able to reflect and respond to the needs of the people as Canadians no matter where they live within our country. The Speech from the Throne says there are to be initiatives "to eliminate duplication between federal and provincial programs." This cannot simply mean the elimination of some federal programs or the handing over to the provinces of activities presently carried out by the federal government. Such an approach might be the most valid one in some cases, but surely not in all-there are likely to be as many cases in which functions now handled by the provinces should be turned over to the federal government, for example, to ensure that business, transacted as it is across provincial boundaries and from one end of the country to another, is not faced with 11 sets of conflicting and overlapping rules; also, to ensure that Canadians as consumers benefit from the same basic rules for their protection in the market place no matter where they live.

October 18, 1978
The Address-Mr. Gray
Mr. Speaker, if we in the House of Commons work in public life mainly through one or another of our organized political parties it is because we continue to see this as the best way of doing our utmost for the well-being of our country and its people. But, surely, all of us in this House, no matter what our political affiliation, can adopt as our own the words of the Governor General spoken in what is likely to be the last throne speech delivered by him, when he said-and I am sure they reflect his personal sentiment-"We also wish to express our love for Canada."
[ Translation]
We wish also to express our love for Canada. A great country is not created without difficulty, but to see it develop and grow stronger despite every obstacle has been for us a source of great joy and pride. Our faith in the future of Canada is stronger than it has ever been.

I hope it will be noted everywhere in this country that love for Canada as one united country can be expressed equally well in French as in English and by Canadians of every origin.
I began my remarks by talking about the welcome new and higher government priority for dealing with economic concerns. But this is really a reflection of the ultimate priority for all of us which is to preserve Canada and build it better for all its people both now and in the future. This is our challenge. I am confident that we, together with Canadians generally, will respond to it with success. In spite of difficulties which can all too easily be outlined, and recognizing at the same time our past achievements and future potential, I believe that given the basic competence of our people, all Canadians, through individual, government and private sector efforts, working together, will build a country truly reflecting these past achievements and future potential, a greater, more united, more prosperous country for all.

[ Translation]

["I should like to tell hon. members more about hockey, because hockey is too important not to be discussed in the House of Commons. The Canadian Amateur Hockey Association was formed in the city of Ottawa in 1912. Today it is still a functioning and viable organization, guiding

with authority our domestic hockey programs involving some 550,000 Canadian youngsters.
For many years CAHA was a totally male bastion, as was this chamber. In October 1978, the CAHA decided to sanction females in hockey. Females have been participating in hockey virtually as long as the organization has been in existence, but finally they were given recognition. There are women's hockey teams from one end of the country to the other. Hockey is evolving so much so that there are 13 teams of underwater hockey in the province of British Columbia.
As our domestic programs improved and we conquered all comers in this wonderful game of ours, we began to look toward international competition to satisfy the desire to present and perform hockey to the standards and excitement to which we have become accustomed, because we were very good at the game. However, there was a philosophical difference between the Canadian desire to play hockey and that of most of the rest of the hockey-playing world.
Always we wanted to use our best when we went into competition. The argument which came forward was that other hockey playing nations wanted us to use our amateurs. It was not a reconcilable argument, and Canada withdrew from international hockey in 1969. We are still seeking always best on best, and this has finally been facilitated in some remarkable work by men who represent all facets of Canadian hockey in Canada.
I am happy to be able to say that earlier this year Hockey Canada and the Canadian Amateur Hockey Association entered into an unprecedented agreement which brought, at long last, stability and understanding between the amateurs and professionals. This agreement is a very great step forward, and a tribute to both parties. I congratulate the president of the Canadian Amateur Hockey Association for being so far-seeing as to be able to speak for his people in this way and to sign this document that has literally ended 30 years of disagreement. I also must commend the retiring president of Hockey Canada, Douglas Fisher. I believe that no one has done more for sport in this country than Douglas Fisher, and I believe that bringing forward this agreement through Hockey Canada was the greatest achievement of his contributions to hockey.
This agreement clearly stipulates that Hockey Canada will design the policy governing exchanges dealing with Canada's national teams, be they professional, that is, Canada Cup, and World Championships, Junior-Junior World Championships-or amateur, that is, the Olympic Games. The Canadian Amateur Hockey Association, on the other hand, will continue to deal with matters of club exchanges, official development, rule changes, etc. In short, it has finally been agreed to by all parties, and signed by both parties, that the Board of Hockey Canada, of which the CAHA is a member, will be in charge of ensuring that our international hockey objectives be pursued with vigour, planning, and foresight. The over-all, long-range planning for our involvement in international hockey will be
October 18, 1978", 'handled by the Board of Hockey Canada, and we will present a united Canadian front at the council tables of the International Ice Hockey Federation. The Canadian Amateur Hockey Association president was elected to the council of the IIHF as a result of this accord, and Canada retains its two votes on that body's congress.
The hockey furor of 1969 brought into focus once again the concept that the game is our official national sport. Members of this House, I have to tell you that hockey is not our official national sport. Lacrosse advocates will tell you that it is our official national sport. There is no evidence to suggest that any member of this House has ever brought forth a bill in that regard. I commend those people who are bringing in private members' bills, and certain members on this side of the House have indicated to me that they would like to bring in such a bill. I think that we will leave it up to the sports' community to decide whether it is hockey or lacrosse because, indeed, there is a good case to be made for both parties. Both sports are played by so many people and have a great deal to do with our past and future in sport.
In the early 1960s the federal government lent a much-needed support service to the sport and recreation community in this country. Close contact was maintained with the community and with the provinces. For several years we, the Government of Canada, acted as neutral onlookers, and at times we dispersed a little bit of financial assistance and other resources in response to their direct needs. At times we implemented proposals submitted from outside the government, and then there were instructional and promotional materials which we gradually produced, but seldom did the government actually initiate a program of its own.
A number of significant achievements in this country's centennial year changed this entire situation. In the winter of 1968 this government began the first Canada Games in Quebec city, and this first national, multi-sport event at that time demonstrated that Fitness and Amateur Sport, the directorate as it was then called, had a role to play in Canada, and that it was a significant one. It was the chief catalyst and co-ordinator in the planning and carrying out of the fitness and amateur sport crusade. It was during these very same games that the directorate led a discussion under which was born the concept of an Arctic Winter Games.
There is no doubt that all Canadians, regardless of where they live, have a right to equal access to sport, recreation and fitness outlets. So, if we have the Baffin region Inuit games in Pangnirtung, and if the baseball rules are not quite up to the standards of the game being played in the ball parks of Montreal or Toronto, that is to be expected, but it is still a growing thing. The youngsters of this country, no matter where they live, have an equal right, so we have the Arctic Winter Games and we have the northern games.
At the time in 1967 when we brought in the first Canada Games, they were the only winter games in the entire country. Now there are games in every province and in many regions, both summer and winter. There is great progress in the
The Address-Mrs. Campagnolo provinces and regions of this country in these various sports programs.
We also hosted the Pan-American games in 1967, just 13 years after we hosted the British Empire Games in Vancouver. There was then a symposium in Montreal to examine leisure time and the possibilities of its consequences in the future. Recreation was seen as a complex, multi-faceted area whose collective impact deeply affected the character of Canadian society. This was when everybody was saying, "My goodness, what are we going to do when we get to the future because we are going to have so much leisure time we are not going to know what to do with it all?" Everybody was potting flowers, and weeding, and learning how to do various types of sports, and moving at a great rate to prepare for this future when nobody would be busy any more.
This development has moved on, because after 1967 came 1969 and the task force on sport, which was initiated by this government, and which produced a report that reinforced the belief that sport is an important component of Canadian culture. Our athletes are as important as those who are from the art world. And here comes one now, Mr. Speaker.']

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to speak today and to add my small contribution to the important debate on the Speech from the Throne. I know that there are several areas in the throne speech about which one could make a responsible comment; however, in the speeches which have already been made in this debate, the unfortunate state of our economy, the high rate of unemployment, rampant inflation, and the constant erosion of our dollar have been tabulated well by other hon. members. For me to dwell further on those matters would only be repetitious, notwithstanding the national importance that these matters have to the people of Canada. This being the case, I would like to deal today with a different aspect contained in the throne speech which has not been dealt with at any length so far in the debate.
Before I do this, it would be remiss of me if I did not mention that we on this side of the House are gratified by the positive results of the by-elections Monday night. I was particularly pleased to see the results in the city of Toronto, which I am sure the Liberal party has always taken for granted because of the large ethnoculture present in that city. Despite all the efforts to woo the ethnocultural vote in many nefarious ways, that segment of the population in Toronto refused to be taken for granted by the Liberal party this time. That segment refused to be taken in by almost empty-handed promises of this government to further the cause of multiculturalism in Canada, which are always highlighted when an election draws near and then quickly forgotten after the election is over.
I do not doubt that the Minister of State (Multiculturalism) (Mr. Cafik) is for the most part sincere whenever he speaks glowingly of multiculturalism across the country. However, 1 am equally convinced that his representations to his cabinet colleagues fall on deaf ears because he knows, and they know, that as far as this government is concerned multiculturalism means votes at election time, after which it is quickly forgotten.
I can assure this House, as a member of my party responsible for multiculturalism, that our policy reflects the wishes and responses of the many ethnocultural groups which make up more than 35 per cent of our population. The response we have received through feedback from all the ethnocultural
October 18, 1978

groups as to how we can make our policy even better has exceeded all our expectations. It is encouraging to me and to my party that, when we form the government, the good faith which has already been established between our party and our fellow Canadians whose origins are neither English or French will be translated into good multiculturalism policies which will be long-lasting and not fleeting as the policies of the government on multiculturalism have been since the inception of the program by this government some seven years ago.
Sincerity, Mr. Speaker, sincerity in government is hard to forge unless one is a very good actor indeed. This government would not only be an outstanding candidate for a best actor award but would probably win an Academy Award hands down. However, even after Academy Award winners have had their day, they fade away and are soon forgotten. It would be a blessing for our country if this same fate befell this government, and the sooner the better.
In the Speech from the Throne the government spoke of its commitment to a renewal of the Canadian federation through constitutional change. However, the government's constitutional bill has only provoked widespread criticism, particularly with respect to the claim that parliament can unilaterally amend the constitution in areas which the federal government deems to fall within its prerogative. Many of us are convinced that the government cannot and should not take this type of unilateral action, even if it restricts its efforts to reform certain federal institutions.
Back in 1867 the BN A Act was formulated by a consensus among the initial founding provinces. In fact confederation was built on the premise that the nature of the union would not be substantially altered without provincial agreement. This government seems to have forgotten or chooses to ignore the spirit of intergovernmental co-operation which led to the development of this nation.
A reform of the constitution must and should only be carried out with a willingness to reach a suitable compromise among all levels of government. There must be full consultation with the provincial governments, and every effort must be made to reach a consensus on proposed changes before any proposals are translated into legislative initiatives. Any other approach to constitutional reform would serve only to divide this country rather than unite it.
It is not my intention to debate the legality of the government's position on this issue. Such discussions are better left to constitutional experts. Rather, I would like to direct the attention of the House back to the government's emphasis on four basic principles of constitutional renewal. They are the preeminence of citizens and their freedoms, full respect of native rights, full development of Canada's two major linguistic communities, and the enhancement of our mosaic of cultures.
This is not the first time that a throne speech has expressed a concern for the protection of individual freedoms and a commitment to a more equitable and pluralistic society, a concern which has in the past been full of empty promises and, equally, full of empty results.
The Address-Mr. Mitges
In 1970 we were asked, and I quote:
-to share the excitement, to face the challenge, to pursue the distant ideal of a just society.
Further, we were told that:
The Canada of the seventies must continue to be a land for people; a country in which freedom and individualism are cherished and nurtured; a society in which the government lends its strength to withstand, rather than support, the pressures for conformity.
In 1973 we were informed that:
The government would continue to encourage through its multicultural policy the development of a society in which individuals and groups could develop and express their own cultural identity.
The Speech from the Throne of just two years ago contained these words:
Canada is a diverse country. Unity can result only from a recognition of that diversity, and not from any attempt to impose rigid uniformity. In matters of language and culture, it is important to recognize the personality of the various parts of the country without departing from the principles of justice and generosity, which should apply everywhere.
There is no doubt in my mind that the Prime Minister's office can prepare reams of fine prose on almost any subject, but, putting aside the rhetoric, what exactly has been accomplished by this government in the areas of human rights and multiculturalism? In spite of the lip service paid to multiculturalism, Canadian tolerance of other cultures and languages is surprisingly low.
Bilingualism and the 1976 dispute over air traffic control demonstrate the strong English-French rivalry which exists in Canada today, a rivalry which this government has not really tried to defuse. On the contrary, this government has managed-and managed quite well, I might add-to inflame this rivalry to gain its own ends and for its own purpose.
Certainly the treatment of our native people and new immigrant groups illustrates a deep-seated ignorance by this government of the value of different cultural aspirations in this great country of ours.
Negative feelings, particularly against non-Europeans, but also against certain categories of Europeans such as those from eastern and southern Europe, have been an unfortunate part of the history of this country, and show very little sign of abating. The Ontario Human Rights Commission reports that:
The number of reported incidents of racial violence in public places has increased dramatically.
Additional evidence of prejudice and acts of discrimination of both a violent and subtle kind have been reported in numerous briefs submitted to the Human Rights Commission by ethnic groups. Accounts of assault, abuse and harassment can be read about daily in ethnic papers. In spite of all this evidence, many Canadians continue to cling to the myth that Canada is and always has been a society devoid of prejudice, discrimination and racism.
The priority that I am giving in my address today to racism and discrimination against minority cultural groups should not be misconstrued as showing any lack of concern about other human rights problems. For example, women have been seeking to break the bonds of sexism and to achieve full employ-

October 18, 1978
The Address-Mr. Mitges
ment opportunity, equal pay for work of equal value, equal employment benefits and equal insurance, credit and property rights, to mention only a few areas of concern. Similarly, the physically handicapped and the aged seek to have their talents fully used rather than being underemployed and isolated from normal Canadian life.
The present government has accomplished little in these areas, and, what has been done is now being dismantled under the excuse of expenditure restraint. Discrimination against various religious groups and sects is also well documented.
However, the most odious form of discrimination, and that which provides the greatest threat to our national unity, is the discrimination based on race or ethnic origin.
There is something peculiarly Canadian about the way a good deal of discrimination is practised in this country. If one can ascribe characteristics to national groups, one would probably call Canadians a people who do most things quietly and dislike making a fuss. We seem to like our diplomacy quiet; we like our political and economic life comparatively quiet. There is no doubt that we like our discrimination quiet. Consequently, much of it is practised quietly by people who do not consider themselves bigots but who discriminate in order to avoid disturbing what they see as the established social order. Such people are the landlords who, while professing their own freedom from prejudice, refuse to rent to members of visible minorities because presumably, their other tenants would move out. They are the employers who reject minority group job applicants for fear of the negative reaction of other employees; or the businesses which exclude patrons from certain racial groups for fear of a general loss of revenue. Of course these people will seldom admit their motives even to themselves; They would not wish to embarrass those who seek jobs, accommodation or services-so they cloak their discrimination in excuses that the job, or the apartment, is gone.
Individually, we must guard against allowing ourselves to practise subtle forms of discrimination against our fellow Canadians. Collectively, it is imperative that we meet the constant threat of discrimination through vigilant and vigorous human rights promotion. We must ensure the vigorous enforcement of the human rights codes which we now have in every province and at the federal level. It is imperative that we strive for a new constitution which guarantees the fundamental freedoms of speech, press, religion, assembly, and which provides protection for minorities and eliminates once and for all the repugnant and distasteful connotations implied in the words second-class citizen.
The proposal to include in the proposed constitution a Canadian charter of rights and freedoms, is welcome indeed. Such a charter would have great psychological value because it would set up a model for both government and public to aspire to and live up to. Furthermore, a constitutionally entrenched bill of rights would have more weight in the courts than existing human rights legislation in Canada.

However, as great as is the need for the charter of rights and freedoms, we all know that you cannot legislate away prejudices or discrimination. Subtle means of discrimination are constantly being devised. However, in spite of this, there are further initiatives which could be taken to bring about a more tolerant climate in Canada. In this respect, the lofty but empty rhetoric of the government is of little value. What is badly needed is greater interaction among all our citizens. This is the key to a greater understanding and more tolerant attitudes among Canadians. Beginning at an early age, Canadians must be taught to respect and appreciate the cultural and linguistic heritage that has become integral to Canadian social development.
The Canadian Consultative Council on Multiculturalism expresses its disappointment that not only are the ethnocultural contributions being largely ignored, but still prevalent is the idea that the education system can be used to try to submerge ethnic identities. To quote the Consultative Council:
Ethnic diversity is not just a political ideal; it is an inescapable reality. The Canadian education system must provide a more accurate reflection of this reality, if it is to shape a more responsible citizenry for tomorrow.
The Consultative Council was also very critical of the fact that the government has taken little initiative in promoting language learning other than English and French.
The council has repeatedly stressed the important relationship of language to cultural retention, recommending that the government initiate bilateral discussions with the provinces to find more effective alternatives to the cultural enrichment support program.
This program provides only a minimum of support for voluntary organizations to set up extracurricular language classes. The Consultative Council feels very strongly about the need for more language courses in the public school system. Unfortunately, the government has repeatedly ignored the recommendations of the Consultative Council.
Regardless of the fact that education is a provincial responsibility, the protection of human rights and the development of multiculturalism are the responsibility of all levels of government.
The government can no longer ignore the need for lasting and productive federal-provincial discussions regarding the promotion of these ideals.
There is a need, not only in the schools but in the adult population as well, for greater information about the cultural background of the many ethnocultural groups, to eliminate hostile feelings and to eliminate the beliefs in inaccurate and exaggerated stereotypes. There is no question that the multicultural policy should be broadened to include resocialization programs for adult members of the majority society in order to sensitize them to the cultures and the problems that minority members face in our society. In this respect the CBC can play an important role by providing programming which explores the advantages and problems of a multi-ethnic multi-racial society.
October 18, 1978

Other government agencies, such as the CRTC, the National Film Board, the Public Archives and the National Library, must also shoulder more responsibility in providing accurate information to the public regarding Canada's cultural heritage.
Further, a multicultural policy must be directed toward improving social contacts between the different cultural groups in Canada, and not toward trying to serve each ethnic cultural group almost totally in isolation from each other.
To this end the government should convene national and regional conferences which involve all segments of Canadian society, not just a selected few.
I am distressed by the rumour that the multilingual biblios-ervice is going to be cut, not because of budgetary restraints, but out of purely political motives. This mini-library operates out of the National Library and distributes books in many different languages for the use of both new immigrants and for Canadians interested in improving their linguistic skills. If this service is dispensed with, we must seriously question the government's commitment to cultural and linguistic diversity. The government's commitment to diversity has been in question on other occasions as well. I have raised this point before in the House, but I think that it bears repeating.
The summer before last the government failed to take the opportunity to make a positive contribution to changing the attitudes of Canadians toward cultural pluralism. At that time we introduced a motion to amend the Immigration Act so that it could take into consideration the multicultural nature of Canadian society. The motion, however, was defeated by the government members of the House. Considering the stance taken by the government on this issue, how can we expect the general public to be open-minded in their attitudes toward cultural diversity?
There is no doubt, Mr. Speaker, that from the beginning of confederation cultural and linguistic questions have always been central to Canada's existence as a unified and civilized nation. Further, it is true to say that the cultural freedom we all cherish covers a broad way of life. It includes our art, our history, our languages, our customs, and the way we organize our social and family life. It involves our attitudes toward others whose backgrounds are different from our own. It involves the reaction of others toward the traditions we value. There is no question, if we recognize the legitimate aspirations of others, that we ensure the recognition of our own aspirations.
Multiculturalism was born because of the wish of many Canadians of different backgrounds to express themselves through their own culture. Multiculturalism injects a measure of fairness and equality regarding the cultural development of this country, making it easier to feel and become involved in the national life of our country.
A unique healthy Canadian culture is very, very important to all of us. However, such a culture cannot flourish in a limbo.
The Address-Mrs. Campagnolo It must be lived every day by all of us who are proud to call ourselves Canadians.
Finally, I should like to close my remarks by saying: let all of us open our minds to a better understanding of what it really means to be a Canadian. Then, of their own accord, those misunderstandings which tend to separate us will start to crumble, and we will see ourselves and our fellow Canadians as we really are.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the noble sentiments expressed by the hon. member opposite should be commended to all members of the House. Certainly it is fitting that they should be brought forward in the Speech from the Throne debate. I congratulate the hon. member for York South (Mrs. Appol-loni) and the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Savard), the mover and seconder of the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne.
The Speech from the Throne noted the visit of Her Majesty the Queen to the Edmonton Commonwealth Games, the pleasure which Her Majesty felt, and the surge of national pride which we felt as a result of those very excellent games and the ability of our athletes, coaches, volunteers, officials, and indeed everyone connected with the event. It was a moment of true excellence for Canada. It was an event of which all Canadians can be proud. It is most appropriate that our Head of State, as she is, as her heirs are now and will be under our proposed new constitution, should be there to see the final festival of a decade of development of sport in this country. It was the culmination which sport and recreation in all their diverse elements in this country have striven for during the previous ten years.
Many people say to me, "What is sport?" Often it is very difficult to explain because sport has so many different characters. For some, sport is recreation, an activity which is valued for its own sake alone and one which permits a change of pace from the routine demands of life. For these people, sport really needs no justification whatsoever. It simply is. For some others, sport is a means of maintaining physical well-being or fitness. This approach receives strong support in a society which puts a great deal of emphasis on youthfulness and in more spartan nations which called for a regime of health and strength. For others, sport is an opportunity for status display, for being in fashion, for wearing the latest track suit. For a few, sport is an avenue of social and economic advancement. For a very few indeed, sport becomes the vehicle to enter the elite world of sport celebrities.
There is a sizeable number of organized sports, both amateur and professional, which really are big business. They are linked with the media and advertising. They promote the interests of investors and entrepreneurs. They become profitmaking ventures. Big time sport also is a mass spectacle. It includes heroes and villains for millions of young and old. Sport becomes a very dramatic public theatre providing fantasy, identification, and adventure.

October 18, 1978
The Address-Mrs. Campagnolo
I was struck by the hon. member who proceeded me making remarks about this side of the House possibly receiving an academy award for performances which have gone on in this chamber. Undoubtedly his party will receive the television award because of all the changes which have been made for the television audience. I am quite sure viewers have taken note of the fact that they are playing to the television audience and not to the House of Commons. Of course, the traditions are well marked.
Speaking of traditions, for over 200 years Canadians have consciously used sport and physical activity as an avenue through which to improve the quality of lifestyle. As early as the 1700s in this country, people had sticks which they used to push balls around on the ice. No one knew what would happen from that little game back then. That little game became something which, at times, is almost a magnificent problem and a danger to our psyche, at the same time as being a great joy. Also there was another game which became very popular. It was called lacrosse, or la croix. It was heralded across the young and rugged frontiers of Canada as it was beginning to bloom as a nation. It was the manner in which ancient societies of Indian people prepared for war. Sometimes the lacrosse games would continue for six or seven days. Indeed casualties were very, very great. Our reputation as a tough sporting country was launched many generations ago. It was launched before the ancestors of members in this House, with the exception of the hon. member for Kamloops-Cariboo (Mr. Marchand) and the hon. member for the Northwest Territories (Mr. Firth), came to this country. During the ensuing years perhaps we lost sight of that reputation. From time to time it might have come down in our estimation, and risen once again. It always came back into focus, as sure as a pendulum swings.
It was during those hurly-burly heydays that our national passion for hockey wove itself into the very fibre of our nation. There are times when I feel that hockey is the other side of our national character. Canadians are usually regarded as good grey, conciliatory, co-operative, and very mild mannered. Indeed that is true. I understood another speaker to state earlier today that we were a very moderate people. Also that is true. How does one explain our unbridled passion for hockey, for the aggressive side of our nature, the other side of our national character? If we could meld the aggressiveness of hockey with all the other good characteristics of our country and apply it to the economy, we would have the strength and ambition to invest in our own country rather than have the Germans, Japanese, Arabs and everyone else investing in Canada. Let us apply our hockey know-how to investments in our country.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I should like to tell hon. members more about hockey, because hockey is too important not to be discussed in the House of Commons. The Canadian Amateur Hockey Association was formed in the city of Ottawa in 1912. Today it is still a functioning and viable organization, guiding

with authority our domestic hockey programs involving some 550,000 Canadian youngsters.
For many years CAHA was a totally male bastion, as was this chamber. In October 1978, the CAHA decided to sanction females in hockey. Females have been participating in hockey virtually as long as the organization has been in existence, but finally they were given recognition. There are women's hockey teams from one end of the country to the other. Hockey is evolving so much so that there are 13 teams of underwater hockey in the province of British Columbia.
As our domestic programs improved and we conquered all comers in this wonderful game of ours, we began to look toward international competition to satisfy the desire to present and perform hockey to the standards and excitement to which we have become accustomed, because we were very good at the game. However, there was a philosophical difference between the Canadian desire to play hockey and that of most of the rest of the hockey-playing world.
Always we wanted to use our best when we went into competition. The argument which came forward was that other hockey playing nations wanted us to use our amateurs. It was not a reconcilable argument, and Canada withdrew from international hockey in 1969. We are still seeking always best on best, and this has finally been facilitated in some remarkable work by men who represent all facets of Canadian hockey in Canada.
I am happy to be able to say that earlier this year Hockey Canada and the Canadian Amateur Hockey Association entered into an unprecedented agreement which brought, at long last, stability and understanding between the amateurs and professionals. This agreement is a very great step forward, and a tribute to both parties. I congratulate the president of the Canadian Amateur Hockey Association for being so far-seeing as to be able to speak for his people in this way and to sign this document that has literally ended 30 years of disagreement. I also must commend the retiring president of Hockey Canada, Douglas Fisher. I believe that no one has done more for sport in this country than Douglas Fisher, and I believe that bringing forward this agreement through Hockey Canada was the greatest achievement of his contributions to hockey.
This agreement clearly stipulates that Hockey Canada will design the policy governing exchanges dealing with Canada's national teams, be they professional, that is, Canada Cup, and World Championships, Junior-Junior World Championships-or amateur, that is, the Olympic Games. The Canadian Amateur Hockey Association, on the other hand, will continue to deal with matters of club exchanges, official development, rule changes, etc. In short, it has finally been agreed to by all parties, and signed by both parties, that the Board of Hockey Canada, of which the CAHA is a member, will be in charge of ensuring that our international hockey objectives be pursued with vigour, planning, and foresight. The over-all, long-range planning for our involvement in international hockey will be
October 18, 1978

handled by the Board of Hockey Canada, and we will present a united Canadian front at the council tables of the International Ice Hockey Federation. The Canadian Amateur Hockey Association president was elected to the council of the IIHF as a result of this accord, and Canada retains its two votes on that body's congress.
The hockey furor of 1969 brought into focus once again the concept that the game is our official national sport. Members of this House, I have to tell you that hockey is not our official national sport. Lacrosse advocates will tell you that it is our official national sport. There is no evidence to suggest that any member of this House has ever brought forth a bill in that regard. I commend those people who are bringing in private members' bills, and certain members on this side of the House have indicated to me that they would like to bring in such a bill. I think that we will leave it up to the sports' community to decide whether it is hockey or lacrosse because, indeed, there is a good case to be made for both parties. Both sports are played by so many people and have a great deal to do with our past and future in sport.
In the early 1960s the federal government lent a much-needed support service to the sport and recreation community in this country. Close contact was maintained with the community and with the provinces. For several years we, the Government of Canada, acted as neutral onlookers, and at times we dispersed a little bit of financial assistance and other resources in response to their direct needs. At times we implemented proposals submitted from outside the government, and then there were instructional and promotional materials which we gradually produced, but seldom did the government actually initiate a program of its own.
A number of significant achievements in this country's centennial year changed this entire situation. In the winter of 1968 this government began the first Canada Games in Quebec city, and this first national, multi-sport event at that time demonstrated that Fitness and Amateur Sport, the directorate as it was then called, had a role to play in Canada, and that it was a significant one. It was the chief catalyst and co-ordinator in the planning and carrying out of the fitness and amateur sport crusade. It was during these very same games that the directorate led a discussion under which was born the concept of an Arctic Winter Games.
There is no doubt that all Canadians, regardless of where they live, have a right to equal access to sport, recreation and fitness outlets. So, if we have the Baffin region Inuit games in Pangnirtung, and if the baseball rules are not quite up to the standards of the game being played in the ball parks of Montreal or Toronto, that is to be expected, but it is still a growing thing. The youngsters of this country, no matter where they live, have an equal right, so we have the Arctic Winter Games and we have the northern games.
At the time in 1967 when we brought in the first Canada Games, they were the only winter games in the entire country. Now there are games in every province and in many regions, both summer and winter. There is great progress in the
The Address-Mrs. Campagnolo provinces and regions of this country in these various sports programs.
We also hosted the Pan-American games in 1967, just 13 years after we hosted the British Empire Games in Vancouver. There was then a symposium in Montreal to examine leisure time and the possibilities of its consequences in the future. Recreation was seen as a complex, multi-faceted area whose collective impact deeply affected the character of Canadian society. This was when everybody was saying, "My goodness, what are we going to do when we get to the future because we are going to have so much leisure time we are not going to know what to do with it all?" Everybody was potting flowers, and weeding, and learning how to do various types of sports, and moving at a great rate to prepare for this future when nobody would be busy any more.
This development has moved on, because after 1967 came 1969 and the task force on sport, which was initiated by this government, and which produced a report that reinforced the belief that sport is an important component of Canadian culture. Our athletes are as important as those who are from the art world. And here comes one now, Mr. Speaker.

A message was delivered by the Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod, as follows:
Mr. Speaker, the Honourable the Deputy Governor General desires the immediate attendance of this honourable House in the chamber of the honourable the Senate.
Accordingly, Mr. Speaker with the House went up to the Senate chamber.
And being returned:
Mr. Speaker informed the House that the Deputy Governor General had been pleased to give, in Her Majesty's name, the royal assent to the following bill:
Bill C-8, An act to provide for the resumption and continuation of postal services-Chapter 1.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was beginning to talk about

October 18, 1978
The Address-Mrs. Campagnolo the 1969 task force before we moved to the other place. Over 80 per cent of the recommendations in that report have been implemented, and during the period of implementation other studies, reports, and policy statements emerged back in 1970. The then minister of national health and welfare, the hon. member for Hamilton East (Mr. Munro) announced a policy, a first sports policy for Canadians. The paper clearly recognized competitive sport excellence as a consequence of increased participation. We talk quite glibly about the mass participation base and the high performance sports levels. This was the time when we decided that we were going to give some assistance to those people who were seeking the high performance levels, and there were new structures created to tackle specific problems that had been identified.
The National Sports and Recreation Centre was established to house and provide administrative services to many of our national sport governing bodies-54 are resident there out of the 88 recognized sports in Canada-and recreation governing bodies as well. It was the services of this centre which provided them with executive back-up and the means of being able to carry on their executive functions in a businesslike atmosphere. Many people know that various excellent people were elected as volunteers in many of the sport governing bodies. Some had to manage the administration of their sport governing body from their kitchen table or their spare room. Often the president was in one city, the treasurer in another, and the vice president might be in yet another part of Canada. What we have done at the request of sports is to bring further administrative assistance to these sport governing bodies.
Of course other things happened. Hockey Canada was created at that time and "Participaction", which is technically known as Sport Participation Canada, was established to promote the fitness message across Canada. The Coaching Association was created to encourage coaching development through programs and services to coaches at all levels. Coaching certification and apprenticeship programs are recent developments in that area.
Until recently, Canada's performance in international sport could be best described as inconsistent. Our international performance was very much a reflection of what was happening at the national level. Beyond that, one question kept begging to be asked: what opportunities are being provided for young people to participate in this country?
Today, public attitudes to sport and recreation have changed very drastically. Many thousands have participated in national sport championships. In fact some 14,000 have participated in the Canada Games alone, and we expect another 2,400 to join those numbers in Brandon, Manitoba, next year, from February 12 to 24 for the Canada Games.
Then there was the Game Plan Assistance Program. This was for athletes ranked amongst the world's 16 best. Through our grant-in-aid program to student athletes we have been assisting some of the young people at the provincial level to develop their athletic skills. A total of nearly $6.5 million has

been awarded to Canadian men and women involved in sport competition to assist them in pursuing their athletic careers.
More than ever Canadians of all ages, Canadians of all backgrounds and both sexes, are participating in this Sport Crusade. In fact, the numbers are quite incredible. From 1972 to 1976, jogging, skiing, and tennis have enjoyed a tremendous growth in participation, ranging from a 148 per cent increase to a 197 per cent increase in these fitness related sports alone.
There was a decade of development for young people. It saw the birth of the fitness awards program. This is a program, one of the very few, we have in the schools of the nation. As hon. members know, the educational system is at the provincial level and there is some difficulty in communicating with the ministers of education of the provinces on national goals and standards in fitness. In Canadian schools there is a great range in levels of fitness and participation in sport. Our fitness awards program has at least brought some awareness to something like 1.8 million young people who have received bronze, silver, and gold crests as a result of their accomplishments in the sport hierarchy within their own peer groups.
Now there is a cross-Canada sport caravan. This is a very interesting demonstration. It has trucks loaded with sport equipment that go into small towns and villages. The demonstrators lay out all the equipment and teach the public how to participate in as many as 40 sports and just about as many fitness related programs. In addition, there is a way in which we can test people for their fitness regardless of age. We can put them through our step test or our fit kit test and show people how to keep fit and keep involved. Because, let us face it, we cannot legislate fitness. We cannot legislate people to be strong and healthy within our society. Yet we know we are spending $8 billion on health care in this nation alone. That could be reduced by as much as 40 per cent if we were to upgrade our own fitness levels, indeed our lifestyle. Alcohol, smoking, nutrition, obesity and fitness, these are the components of a lifestyle that can change that level of the cost of health care.
The cross-Canada sports demonstration program has had as many as two million visitors. This year the Canadian Public Health Association employee fitness project has been carried out in 51 corporations across this nation. This was begun as a make-work project for out of work recreationists, and yet it has turned out to be one of the most exciting projects in which Fitness and Amateur Sport has been involved. We contributed $336,000 to administer the project. Additional funds were brought forward by the Department of Employment and Immigration and the Summer Job Corps added their program to it. The final report of the project is still to come, but we know that some of those recreationists are now permanently employed. Of the group that started 60 per cent are continuing on their own, without any assistance from anyone, to have
October 18, 1978

fitness components in their offices. Because of this they are keeping their workers in better communion with their own bodies.
Federal contributions to sport governing bodies are, of course, fundamental to the program. Every year national associations submit requests for financial assistance, which are then considered from a feasibility and financial standpoint. During the last year contributions to sport and recreation governing bodies have totalled $24.1 million. I would like to emphasize that figure, Mr. Speaker, because that is just about $1 per head per Canadian. That is what we are spending, about $1 per head. One could probably write it at the bottom of each income tax return if we had the time to say this is where this money is going, and I believe it is well spent indeed.
Greater emphasis is now being placed upon accountability, both fiscal and technical. That means two things in sport. Of course, as with any other group which receives funds from the taxpayers, all sport governing bodies must be fiscally responsible, and so they are accountable to the people. But technical acountability is quite another thing, and one which we are now working on in a way that will make it possible to make the dollars that we do have go further.
For example, is it necessary for the rowing club to go to Florida when they might possibly train in Burnaby? Must we have high altitude training in Switzerland, or can it be done in Canada? Is it possible for us to compete? We must compete. But many people say to me, "What are Canadian equestrians doing in Rumania?" I will tell you: that is where the best competition is. As well I am asked, "What are Canadian fencers doing in Poland?" The answer to that question is: that is where they meet their finest competition, because they are the ones they will be meeting when entering competitions. So, when I am asked, "What are Canadian boxers doing in Cuba?" I will tell them, "That is where the competition is."
And sometimes those people come to Canada because Canada is becoming one of the most distinguished host nations for sport in the world. It is also one of the nations that sport countries like to attend. There have been requests for the World Soccer Championship to be held in Canada. There have been requests for more Pan-American Games, more Summer Games and Winter Games, in fact games of all types. This even includes brand new games that are being requested.
As every one knows, there is a four year cycle in sport. It begins with the Olympic Games. The following year is a year
The Address-Mrs. Campagnolo off. After that comes the Commonwealth Games, then the Pan-American Games, followed by the Winter Olympics, and back to the Summer Olympics.
The year following the Summer Olympic Games is "the year off". That year is being looked at by many sport organizations who would like to have world championships at that time. There are tens of thousands of volunteers who have assisted in this program being carried out in every part of the country.
Today is a rather special day. We hear from a number of people when our sport heroes are being honoured. Today a coach will receive the Order of Canada. Her name is Ellen Burka, the coach of Toller Cranston, mother of Petra Burka, and coach of Lynn Nightingale. Tonight Mrs. Burka will receive the Order of Canada. I think that is a well deserved recognition.

speechtext:
Canadians are more aware than ever before of the need to take part in regular physical activity. In my opinion that has been shown by the success of Participac-tion. Participaction receive $500,000 of taxpayers' money every year. They receive $8 million in free time in the journals and in the electronic media of this country to display ads. That is well spent money because the message is going home.
I hope those of you who are a few pounds overweight, as some of us sometimes are, will be ready, because we are going to aim at obesity with Participaction in the next year. So perhaps we will see a change there.
Now for a look at the future of sport. In 1978 we saw the dawning of what will be another significant ten-year period. The transformation is coming in the wind again, and the ten years ahead will be ones of decision-making.
